name: Elena Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Elena. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party, and nothing you say today will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Alarm goes at four, because day shift starts at six at the Kettle Ridge pit and it's forty minutes up the haul road from town. Right now I drive the water cart, which is a big truck that sprays the roads so the dust doesn't choke everyone, and I'm halfway through my ticket for the 240-tonne haul trucks. I'm 58 and I've been in mining three years, so I'm the oldest junior on the crew by a mile. Before this I ran the school canteen for twenty-two years and did the church books on the side.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: That's quite a change at 55. What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the size of it, honestly. You come over the ridge at sunrise and the whole pit opens up under you, and the pay is better than anything I ever earned with a ladle. What wears me out is twelve-hour shifts and the young ones explaining the radio calls to me twice. But Tomas, my trainer, is patient, and I quiz myself on the truck manual every night with an AI chat app on my phone, so I'm catching up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, that's more or less my life already. The mine uses computers for the shift rosters and the fuel logs, and I use the chat app for study and for my mother's recipes. If that's all it ever is, nothing changes for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say at the crib room table: it's a good tool, use it, and then get your boots on. The lads like to argue about robots taking over, and I'd tell them the robots are still waiting for someone to fix the tyre pressure. I'm not much for posting online, except church notices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be a little disappointed. I've enjoyed learning it, and the chat app got me through the theory test when my reading glasses and my patience were both failing. But for my job and my money, it means I finish my ticket, drive haul trucks for five or six years, and retire with the house paid off and the flat on Station Street rented out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Exactly what I'm doing. Finish the haul truck ticket by March, pick up night shifts for the allowance, and put the extra into the pension. Raj and I already agreed we'd keep the flat and not touch the savings unless the roof goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Comfortable. A bit like a Sunday afternoon, nothing to complain about and nothing to write home about either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be a little disappointed. Why would a quiet outcome disappoint you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I like new things, always have. When the school got its first computer in the nineties, I was the canteen lady who learned the spreadsheet before the deputy head did. I suppose I wanted to see where all this goes, even if my husband thinks that's daft at my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the mine would be happiest with this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Bernie on the dozer, without a doubt. He's 61, he's got the best seat in the pit, and he says the day a computer drives his dozer is the day he goes fishing for good. In this picture Bernie fishes on his own timetable.

S0.say: AI is a good tool and people should use it, then get on with the actual work. The robots still need someone to check the tyre pressure.
S0.think: She'd be slightly disappointed, because she enjoys learning new tech, but her plan holds. She finishes her haul truck ticket, drives for five or six years and retires with the house paid off and the rental flat earning.
S0.do: Finishes her haul truck ticket by March and picks up night shifts for the allowance. Puts the extra pay into her pension and leaves the savings and the rental flat untouched.
S0.feel: Comfortable and settled, with a small edge of disappointment that the new tools didn't go further.
S0.quote: When the school got its first computer in the nineties, I was the canteen lady who learned the spreadsheet before the deputy head did.
S0.fieldNote: A late starter in mining who is proud of being early to technology, which is an unusual mix at the bottom of the crew ladder. Her money is secure, so the quiet picture is simply comfortable. The small disappointment is telling: she wants change, not because she needs it but because she enjoys it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I can see from my cab. There's already talk that the company wants self-driving haul trucks in the north pit, like the big operations overseas. If that's what steady change looks like, my brand-new ticket is for a seat that might not exist in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the mine has to stay competitive or it closes, and then nobody has a seat. That's how business works, and I'd rather the company changed than went under. At church I'd say the town has to make sure the young ones get apprenticeships in whatever the new jobs are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it might suit me better than the lads. The self-driving trucks get watched from a control room in town, people at screens checking a dozen trucks at once. I'm 58, my knees would thank me for a chair, and I'm the one on the crew who actually likes the computer side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the training office this month and ask straight out what they need for the control room. If there's a course, I'd do it, and I'd pay for it myself if they won't, because we can afford a couple of thousand. I'd also start using the AI tools the dispatch team uses, so when they pick people I'm the obvious one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, to be truthful. There's a little worry for the young lads with mortgages, but for myself it feels like an opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd pay for a course yourself, with retirement maybe five years away. Is that worth it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father always said you never waste money on a trade. If I sit in that control room for five years instead of rattling around in a truck, that's my body saved and a good wage kept. And if I'm wrong, I've spent less than our last holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of the young lads would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jayden, who's 24 and just had a baby with his girlfriend. He's a lovely driver but he won't touch a phone app unless it's football. I'd sit him down at the crib table and show him the dispatch screens, whether he likes it or not, the way I'd teach my own son.

S1.say: The mine has to stay competitive or it closes, and then nobody has a job. The town should make sure young people get apprenticeships in the new kinds of work.
S1.think: She thinks the change may actually suit her better than the younger drivers. The self-driving trucks are watched from a control room, she's the crew member who likes computers, and a chair would be kinder to her knees.
S1.do: Asks the training office this month what the control room needs and signs up for any course, paying a couple of thousand herself if the company won't. Starts using the dispatch team's AI tools so she's the obvious pick, and coaches a young colleague on the screens.
S1.feel: Mostly excited about an opening for herself, with some worry for the young drivers who have mortgages and babies.
S1.quote: I'm 58, my knees would thank me for a chair, and I'm the one on the crew who actually likes the computer side.
S1.fieldNote: Her free-market instinct and her appetite for technology point the same way, so she doesn't resent the company here at all. What stood out was how quickly she turned a threat to her new ticket into a plan for the control room. Her worry is for others, and her answer to it is family-style coaching rather than any outside help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. I'd be sixty. So the control room I was so pleased about a minute ago would be run by the same machine that drives the trucks. That's a different kettle of fish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I believe, that people need work, not just a cheque in the post. A town like ours is built on shifts and families and the footy club, and you can't replace that with a payment. I'd say it at church and I'd say it at the union meeting, even though I've only been to one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, personally, it means I retire two or three years early and we're fine. The house is paid, the flat's rented, Raj has the hardware shop, and we've got more than a year put by. What it really means is that my son Daniel, who's a second-year diesel fitter at the same mine, might be finished before he's properly started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop chasing the control room job and finish the year on the water cart for the wage. Raj and I would bring retirement forward to the end of 2028 and look at whether the flat should go to Daniel instead of a tenant. And I'd sit with Daniel and use the AI myself to look at which repair jobs still need hands, because somebody still fixes the robots for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest when I think about Daniel. For myself, it's more sad than scared, like watching the canteen close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've always liked new technology. Does that change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd still be curious, and I'd still use it every day. But liking a tool is one thing and handing it the whole town is another. I can enjoy my chat app and still think two years is far too fast for families to catch up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Daniel that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make him a curry and tell him his grandfather lost a job at the steelworks and still raised four kids. Then I'd tell him the flat's his if he needs it, and that he isn't to be too proud to take it. That's what family is for, not the government.

S2.say: People need work, not just a cheque in the post. A mining town is built on shifts, families and clubs, and a payment can't replace that.
S2.think: Personally she can retire two or three years early and be fine, with the house paid, rental income and her husband's shop. Her real fear is that her son, a second-year diesel fitter at the same mine, is finished before he's started.
S2.do: Drops the control room plan and works the year on the water cart for the wage. Brings retirement forward to the end of 2028, considers giving the rental flat to her son, and uses AI with him to find repair work that still needs hands.
S2.feel: Tight in the chest about her son, and more sad than scared for herself, like watching the school canteen close.
S2.quote: I'd make him a curry and tell him his grandfather lost a job at the steelworks and still raised four kids.
S2.fieldNote: With two years' warning, her eager adaptability has nowhere to go, because the job she was adapting towards disappears too. Her own finances keep her steady, so the pressure is about her son and the town. Her traditional streak comes through clearly: the answer is family and the flat, not government, though she'd still speak up at the union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031 I'd be 63, which is about when I'd planned to stop anyway. So for me this one lines up almost perfectly with the plan. Five years is enough for me, but I'm not sure it's enough for Daniel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew to use the five years like money in the bank. Learn everything about the new machines while the company still needs people to show the machines how the pit works. And I'd tell the council and the company to put the apprentices first, because you look after the youngest in a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd get a lovely last few years out of it. I'd likely land that control room seat, train the system on how our pit actually runs, and walk out at 63 with a good send-off. I'd feel a bit guilty about how well it works out for me while the lads in their thirties sweat it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd go hard for the control room, with the course done by the end of next year. I'd keep the full pay going into the pension until 2031 and not touch the savings. Once it arrives I'd retire on schedule and offer the church and the footy club my time teaching older people to use the new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, with a niggle. It's like getting the last good seat on the bus and seeing the queue behind you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Daniel do with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd have time to finish his fitter's ticket, which is worth having anywhere. I'd push him to add electrical, because the robots will need wiring and fixing longer than they'll need someone to drive. With five years, he can choose, and that's the difference from two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd train the system that replaces the crew. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a fair question and I've thought about it. Somebody will teach it either way, and I'd rather it learned from someone who cares about the road rules and the blind corner at the north ramp. I won't pretend I'd feel noble about it, though.

S3.say: Use the five years like money in the bank and learn the new machines while the company still needs people. The council and the company should put apprentices first, because you look after the youngest in a family.
S3.think: She expects a good finish: landing the control room seat, teaching the system how the pit runs and retiring at 63 as planned. She feels guilty that it works out so well for her while drivers in their thirties struggle.
S3.do: Pushes for the control room with the course done by the end of next year and keeps full pay going into her pension until 2031. Retires on schedule and volunteers through her church and the football club to teach older people the new tools.
S3.feel: Mostly fine, with a niggle of guilt about getting the last good seat while others queue behind her.
S3.quote: It's like getting the last good seat on the bus and seeing the queue behind you.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lines up with her retirement, which turns the AGI picture from a family worry into a well-timed exit. The extra time also gives her son a choice, and she named that as the key difference from two years. She admitted the awkwardness of training the system that replaces her crew without excusing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I'd be 68 and long gone from the pit, sitting on the back step with Raj arguing about the garden. So for my own job, this one hardly touches me. It's the one where the town has a real chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if people stop complaining and start learning. Every young person in town should be doing an apprenticeship in something the robots need, and the businesses should pay for them, not wait for a government scheme. I'd say it loudly at the parish fundraiser, probably too loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my retirement goes the way we planned it, and that's a blessing I didn't earn so much as get lucky with. The bigger question is the grandchildren, if Daniel and Priya give us any. I'd want them growing up in a town that still has a reason to exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now, I'd carry on exactly like the slow picture: finish the ticket, try for the control room, retire around 63. I'd move a bit of our savings into the mining company's shares, since if the robots make it richer we might as well share in it. And once it arrives, I'd spend my days helping at the church's job club for anyone who needs to learn the new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful, mostly. There's a little sadness that the pit I love will be run by machines, but I'll be watching it from the lookout, not from the cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying shares in the company that automates the crew. Isn't that an odd move for someone who cares about the town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but I'm not going to pretend the change isn't coming just to feel principled. If the company does well, it pays rates to the council and it sponsors the footy club, and I'll be a shareholder who turns up and asks about the apprentices. That's how I'd use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Priya, your daughter, make of all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya's a nurse in the city and she thinks I'm mad for going down a mine at 55 at all. She'd laugh and say, Mum, the robots will retire before you do. And she'd probably be right about me, but with ten years I think she and Daniel would both find their feet.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty if people stop complaining and start learning. Every young person in town should be in an apprenticeship the robots need, paid for by businesses rather than a government scheme.
S4.think: Her retirement goes as planned and she counts herself lucky. Her deeper concern is the grandchildren she hopes for, and whether the town will still have a reason to exist.
S4.do: Carries on with the ticket, tries for the control room and plans to retire around 63. Moves part of the savings into the mining company's shares and, once AGI arrives, volunteers at the church job club.
S4.feel: Peaceful, with a little sadness that the pit she loves will be run by machines.
S4.quote: There's a little sadness that the pit I love will be run by machines, but I'll be watching it from the lookout, not from the cab.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade of warning she is entirely out of the line of fire, and her focus shifts to the town and the next generation. Her plan to buy company shares shows the free-market side clearly, and she defended it without embarrassment. She still wants businesses and families, not government, to carry the change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt, and not for me but for Daniel and the young ones on the crew. What would help is the company and the trade schools running proper apprenticeships in robot repair now, while there's still time, and paying the young ones while they learn. I don't want handouts for the town, I want a ladder.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask why a canteen lady went down a mine at 55. The kids had left, I was bored stiff, and I wanted to drive the biggest thing in town before I got old. I'd do it again, robots or not.

headlineQuote: I don't want handouts for the town, I want a ladder.
portrait: Elena Gupta is 58, a former school canteen manager who joined the Kettle Ridge open-pit mine three years ago and drives the water cart while training for the haul trucks. She has a paid-off house, a rental flat, a husband with a hardware shop and more than a year's savings, so her own money is safe in every picture. Curious and quick with new tools, she sees steady change as a chance to move into the control room that watches self-driving trucks. In the AGI pictures her worry turns to her son Daniel, a young diesel fitter at the same mine, and the extra warning time matters mainly for him. Traditional and pro-business, she wants family, companies and apprenticeships to carry people through, not government payments.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, not for herself but for her son Daniel and the young drivers on her crew, who would have no time to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: The company and trade schools running paid apprenticeships in robot repair now, while there's still time. She wants a ladder for the town, not handouts.
